lede: A Python UDF gets one value at a time. A pandas UDF gets a whole batch of values as a pandas Series, moved between Spark and Python with Apache Arrow, so your function works on a column at once instead of looping.
objectives: Write a pandas UDF with `@F.pandas_udf` that takes pandas Series and returns a Series of the same length
Convert `DECIMAL` columns before arithmetic, and know that NaN in the result becomes NULL
Explain what Arrow moves between Spark and Python, and turn it on for `toPandas()`
Choose between a built-in function, a pandas UDF and a Python UDF

blocks.md:
`daily_prices` has one row per stock per trading day: the `open`, `high`, `low` and `close` prices (as `DECIMAL`) and the `volume` of shares traded.

The Python UDFs of the last lesson are called once per row. Spark packs each value, sends it to a Python process, calls your function, and packs the answer back. A **pandas UDF** is called once per **batch** of rows. Spark sends the batch in Apache Arrow's column format, PySpark turns each column into a pandas `Series`, and your function returns a `Series` of the same length.

Write one with the `@F.pandas_udf("type")` decorator. The type hints `pd.Series -> pd.Series` say this is the Series-in, Series-out kind.

blocks.title: Volume in millions, one batch at a time
blocks.note: `volume / 1_000_000` divides the whole Series in one step; there's no loop. The second function shows the batch: all 14 rows arrived in a single call. On a bigger table Spark sends several batches, one partition at a time.

blocks.md:
Inside the function you write pandas, not Spark. `BIGINT` arrives as `int64`, but a `DECIMAL` column arrives as a Series of Python `Decimal` objects (pandas dtype `object`). Arithmetic on them gives more `Decimal` objects, and Arrow can't turn those into a `double` column.

The function below finds where the close sits in the day's range: 0 means it closed at the low, 1 at the high.

blocks.title: Decimal values into a double result
blocks.note: The result is a Series of `Decimal` objects, and converting it to an Arrow `double` array fails in the Python worker. A Python UDF would have given NULL silently here; a pandas UDF stops with an error.

blocks.md: Convert first: `series.astype("float64")` turns `Decimal` values into floats. Then pandas works as usual, including `.round(2)`. A function can take several columns; Spark passes them in the order you list them.

blocks.title: Convert, compute, round
blocks.note: BRVO.SX closed right at its low on 2026-01-21 (0.1) and CYPH.SX near its high on 2026-01-15 (0.81).

blocks.md:
Missing values need no special code in most pandas UDFs. A NULL `DECIMAL` arrives as `None`, `astype("float64")` turns it into `NaN`, arithmetic with `NaN` gives `NaN`, and **a `NaN` in the returned Series becomes NULL** in Spark.

One rule is strict: the returned Series must have exactly as many values as the input. A shorter or longer result stops the job with an error.

blocks.title: A missing price gives NULL
blocks.code:
import pandas as pd
from decimal import Decimal
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


@F.pandas_udf("double")
def close_position(high: pd.Series, low: pd.Series, close: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    h = high.astype("float64")
    l = low.astype("float64")
    c = close.astype("float64")
    return ((c - l) / (h - l)).round(2)


prices = spark.createDataFrame(
    [
        ("ALDR.SX", Decimal("192.26"), Decimal("186.69"), Decimal("191.95")),
        ("BRVO.SX", None, Decimal("54.08"), Decimal("54.62")),
    ],
    "symbol STRING, high DECIMAL(10,2), low DECIMAL(10,2), close DECIMAL(10,2)",
)
result = prices.select("symbol", close_position("high", "low", "close").alias("close_position"))
result.show()
print(result.filter(F.col("close_position").isNull()).count(), "missing value")
blocks.note: The second row has no `high`, so its result is NULL, not NaN: `isNull()` finds it.

blocks.md:
Arrow helps outside UDFs too. `df.toPandas()` copies a whole DataFrame to the driver as a pandas DataFrame. With `spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled` set to `"true"`, Spark makes that copy in Arrow column batches instead of converting row by row. It's off unless you turn it on, and the result is the same either way.

`toPandas()` puts every row in the driver's memory, so use it only on small results, such as a summary you want to plot.

blocks.title: toPandas with Arrow
blocks.code:
print(spark.conf.get("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled"))
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled", "true")

pdf = daily_prices.toPandas()
print(type(pdf).__name__, pdf.shape)
print(pdf.dtypes)
print(pdf[pdf["symbol"] == "ALDR.SX"][["trade_date", "close", "volume"]])
blocks.note: `pdf` is an ordinary pandas DataFrame with 14 rows and 7 columns. The prices and dates came across as Python objects (dtype `object`); only `volume` became a numeric dtype, so convert prices before pandas arithmetic here too.

blocks.md:
So which tool when?

- **A built-in function** first, always, when one exists: it runs in the JVM and the optimiser can see it.
- **A pandas UDF** when you need Python, especially pandas or NumPy, over whole columns. Values travel in Arrow batches and your code runs vectorised.
- **A Python UDF** for logic that is naturally one value at a time, such as parsing an odd string. Every value is packed and unpacked on its own.

The pandas and Python UDFs below give the same answers; only how the values travel differs.

blocks.title: The same result, two ways
blocks.code:
import pandas as pd
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

per_row = F.udf(lambda v: v / 1_000_000, "double")


@F.pandas_udf("double")
def per_batch(volume: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return volume / 1_000_000


daily_prices.select("symbol", "trade_date", per_row("volume").alias("python_udf"), per_batch("volume").alias("pandas_udf")).show(5)
blocks.note: The Python UDF's lambda ran once per row; the pandas UDF ran once for the batch. On large tables that difference is why pandas UDFs are preferred when you need Python.

concept.prompt: A function is declared with `@F.pandas_udf("double")` and `def f(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series`. What is `s` when Spark calls it?
choices: A batch of the column's values, as one pandas Series
The whole table as a pandas DataFrame
concept.why: Spark sends rows in batches through Arrow, and each argument is that batch of one column as a pandas Series.

concept.prompt: A pandas UDF returns a Series with `NaN` for one row. What does that row hold in the Spark result?
choices: The job stops with an error
concept.why: When the result goes back through Arrow, a `NaN` in the returned Series becomes NULL, so `isNull()` finds it.

concept.prompt: A pandas UDF gets a Series of 14 values and returns a Series of 1 value. What happens?
choices: Spark repeats the value for all 14 rows
Only the first row is kept
The job stops with an error about the result length
concept.why: The result must have exactly as many values as the input. Spark checks, and stops with an error saying it expected 14 and got 1.

review: A pandas UDF (`@F.pandas_udf("type")`, `pd.Series -> pd.Series`) is called once per batch, not once per row.
Spark moves each batch with Arrow and hands every column to your function as a pandas Series.
`DECIMAL` columns arrive as `Decimal` objects: `astype("float64")` before arithmetic, or converting the result fails.
`NaN` in the returned Series becomes NULL. The result must be as long as the input.
`spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled` makes `toPandas()` copy in Arrow batches; `toPandas()` is for small results only.
Prefer built-ins; use a pandas UDF when you need Python over whole columns, and a Python UDF for one-value-at-a-time logic.
